newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Mercedes says new models boost sales.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mercedes says new models boost sales.

text.p: German luxury carmaker Mercedes-Benz AG, boosted by strong demand for new models, said on Friday that it expected higher sales and profits this year and promised record sales in 1997.

Revealing numbers that were in line with analysts' expectations, Mercedes said in a statement that sales in 1996 would climb to 77 billion marks ($50 billion) from 72.03 billion marks the year before.

"The story of 1996 is a story of a strong Mercedes-Benz," chairman Helmut Werner said. "Mercedes has set a target of being number one in innovation, quality and profits. 1997 will be an important step in that direction."
The company said it expected record 1996 car deliveries of more than 640,000 units, up from 590,200. Truck deliveries, meanwhile, should climb to 345,000 units from 320,089.
In 1995, Mercedes net income grew 23 percent to 2.28 billion marks.
Mercedes credited the strong sales growth to four new models introduced during the year, almost uniformly to strong advance orders and favourable evaulations from the motoring press.

Detailing the revenue figures for 1996, Mercedes said it woud report car sales would climb to 46 billion marks from 40.4 billion marks and that truck sales would remain steady around 31 billion marks compared with 31.6 billion marks the year before.
Mercedes said car sales were driven largely by its E-class model, the backbone of its car fleet, and strong demand for its new SLK sports car.
The carmaker said it intended to increase production of the two-seat cabriolet in 1997 to 47,000 units from an originally planned 35,000.
"In no other year of our 100-year history have we had so many new product introductions," Werner said.
Mercedes said the strongest growth had come from the U.S. and Japan were unit car sales should have climbed around 20 percent.
The share price of Mercedes' parent company, Daimler-Benz AG, climbed on the report, trading up 1.25 marks in afternoon trade at 103.85.
The company's truck division, hit by a weak European market, offered a more mixed story.
The operation's stronger sales came largely from demand for its popular vans, the Sprinter and Vito. In the two to six tonne class, new registrations climbed to 118,000 units from 93,100 units.

The statement did not include details of sales for heavy trucks, but Mercedes fortunes in the segment have suffered in recent years from a weak market and tough price competition from competitors such as AB Volvo.

Heavy truck sales, however, could improve in 1997. Earlier this year, Mercedes introduced its hotly awaited Actros line and demand for the new model is likely to improve sales at Mercedes' truck division.
The upbeat report comes during a period of mounting controversy at Mercedes and its parent company Daimler-Benz AG.
Daimler chairman Juergen Schrempp is planning to unveil plans for a wide-ranging reorganisation of the industrial giant in late January -- plans which are expected to reduce Mercedes' independence.
Werner has opposed any threat to his unit's autonomy and many analysts believe he may be forced to leave Mercedes unless a deal is struck over the future of Daimler.
